cultural.vision_reason: This is an ancient Egyptian limestone sculptor's trial piece/ostracon carved with a canine (jackal/dog) head, an artist's practice or model piece from Ptolemaic Egypt, clearly consistent with Egyptian sculptural craft.

physical.title: Double-Sided Votive Relief
physical.summary: Trial pieces—carved on limestone flakes, or ostraca—and sculptors' models allow us to see how the ancient Egyptian artist approached his work. The four heads—a king, a shaven-headed priest, and two foreigners—on this large trial piece were doubtless practice sketches but nonetheless show the learner's keen eye for detail and for distinguishing different facial types. Others, such as the wild dog's head and the profile of a king in relief, are masterpieces in their own right, and were probably meant to be copied. The sculpture of a lion was left unfinished, which makes it even more intriguing; even in its roughed-out-state it is a majestic figure. The back of this piece is carved in the figure of a goddess.

location.made_in_place: Egypt, Greco-Roman period (332 BCE–395 CE), Ptolemaic dynasty (305–30 BCE)
